claim: Most visual tasks involve looking for specific object features.
source: Most visual tasks involve looking for specific object features.
evidence: This is a general statement about visual tasks presented in the introduction without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: In feature-based tasks, we form a template in our brain that helps guide eye movements and locate the target.
source: In such tasks, which have been studied extensively, we form a template in our brain that helps guide eye movements and locate the target (Peelen and Kastner, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peelen and Kastner, 2014.

claim: The degree of match to a template indicates the presence or absence of the desired object in feature-based tasks.
source: This template becomes a decision variable that can be used to solve the task: the degree of match to the template indicates the presence or absence of the desired object (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and established knowledge about decision-making models.

claim: Property-based visual tasks include same-different task, finding the oddball item, and judging if an object has symmetry.
source: Examples of such property-based tasks are same-different task, finding the oddball item and judging if an object has symmetry (Figure 1B).
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Property-based tasks cannot be solved by looking for any particular feature.
source: These tasks cannot be solved by looking for any particular feature, and therefore present a major challenge for standard models of decision making since the underlying feature space and decision variable are unknown.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of property-based tasks.

claim: Machine vision algorithms fail at detecting properties like same-different and at other similar visual reasoning challenges.
source: Even machine vision algorithms, which are so successful at solving feature-based tasks (Serre, 2019), fail at detecting properties like same-different and at other similar visual reasoning challenges (Fleuret et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2018; Ricci et al., 2021; Puebla and Bowers, 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on machine vision limitations.

claim: Visual search, same-different judgments, and symmetry detection have been considered as conceptually distinct tasks in theoretical studies.
source: Even theoretical studies have considered visual search (Verghese, 2001; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017), same-different judgments (Nickerson, 1969; Petrov, 2009) and symmetry detection (Wagemans, 1997; Bertamini and Makin, 2014) as conceptually distinct tasks.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple theoretical studies.

claim: Property-based tasks all involve discriminating between items with repeating features from those without repeating features.
source: However, we note that at a deeper level, these tasks are similar because they all involve discriminating between items with repeating features from those without repeating features.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors about the commonality among tasks.

claim: The neural response to multiple objects is the average of the single object responses according to divisive normalization.
source: According to the well-known principle of divisive normalization in high-level visual cortex (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Agrawal et al., 2020; Katti and Arun, 2022), the neural response to multiple objects is the average of the single object responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on divisive normalization.

claim: The response to an array of identical items will be the same as the response to the single item.
source: Accordingly, the response to an array of identical items will be the same as the response to the single item.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the principle of divisive normalization.

claim: The response to an array containing a target among distractors would lie along the line joining the target and distractor in representational space.
source: Similarly, the response to an array containing a target among distractors, being a mix of images, would lie along the line joining the target and distractor in underlying representational space.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the principle of divisive normalization applied to mixed displays.

claim: Homogeneous (target-absent) arrays naturally stand apart since they contain repeating items.
source: It can be seen that the homogeneous (target-absent) arrays naturally stand apart since they contain repeating items, whereas the heterogeneous (target-present) arrays come closer to each other since they contain a mixture of items.
evidence: This is an inference based on the predicted neural computations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Heterogeneous (target-present) arrays come closer to each other since they contain a mixture of items.
source: It can be seen that the homogeneous (target-absent) arrays naturally stand apart since they contain repeating items, whereas the heterogeneous (target-present) arrays come closer to each other since they contain a mixture of items.
evidence: This is an inference based on the predicted neural computations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Distance from the center of perceptual space can be used to discriminate homogeneous from heterogeneous displays.
source: Since displays with repeating items are further away from the center of this space, this distance can be used to discriminate them from heterogeneous displays (Figure 2C, inset).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesized neural computation with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Both symmetric and asymmetric objects show part summation in their neural responses.
source: Indeed, both symmetric and asymmetric objects show part summation in their neural responses (Pramod and Arun, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pramod and Arun, 2018.

claim: If visual homogeneity is a decision variable, then response times should be slowest for displays with VH close to the decision boundary.
source: First, if VH is being used to solve visual search and symmetry detection tasks, then responses should be slowest for displays with VH close to the decision boundary and faster for displays with VH far away (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a prediction based on decision-making theory.

claim: For target-present arrays and asymmetric objects, response time should be positively correlated with visual homogeneity.
source: This predicts opposite correlations between response time and VH: for target-present arrays and asymmetric objects, the response time should be positively correlated with VH.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesized role of visual homogeneity.

claim: For target-absent arrays and symmetric objects, response time should be negatively correlated with visual homogeneity.
source: By contrast, for target-absent arrays and symmetric objects, response time should be negatively correlated with VH.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesized role of visual homogeneity.

claim: The net correlation between response time and visual homogeneity will be close to zero.
source: Importantly, because response times of the two choices are positively and negatively correlated with VH, the net correlation between response time and VH will be close to zero.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the opposite correlations predicted for the two conditions.

claim: If visual homogeneity is encoded by a dedicated brain region, then brain activity in that region will be positively correlated with VH.
source: Second, if VH is encoded by a dedicated brain region, then brain activity in that region will be positively correlated with VH (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a prediction for brain imaging experiments.

claim: A positive correlation between brain activity and visual homogeneity cannot be explained easily by cognitive processes linked to response time.
source: Such a positive correlation cannot be explained easily by cognitive processes linked to response time such as attention or task difficulty, since response times will have zero correlation with the mean activity of this region.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the predicted zero correlation between VH and RT.

claim: Object representations in high-level visual cortex match strongly with perceived dissimilarity measured in visual search.
source: We drew upon the principle that object representations in high-level visual cortex match strongly with perceived dissimilarity measured in visual search (Sripati and Olson, 2010; Zhivago and Arun, 2014; Agrawal et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In Experiment 1, 16 human participants viewed arrays made from 32 grayscale natural objects with an oddball on the left or right.
source: In Experiment 1, 16 human participants viewed arrays made from a set of 32 grayscale natural objects, with an oddball on the left or right (Figure 3A), and had to indicate the side on which the oddball appeared using a key press.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: Participants in Experiment 1 were highly accurate in their responses (accuracy: 98.8 ± 0.9%).
source: Participants were highly accurate and consistent in their responses during this task (accuracy, mean ± sd: 98.8 ± 0.9%; correlation between mean response times of even- and odd-numbered participants: r=0.91, p<0.0001 across all 32C2=496 object pairs).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Response times in Experiment 1 were consistent across participants (r=0.91, p<0.0001).
source: Participants were highly accurate and consistent in their responses during this task (accuracy, mean ± sd: 98.8 ± 0.9%; correlation between mean response times of even- and odd-numbered participants: r=0.91, p<0.0001 across all 32C2=496 object pairs).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The reciprocal of response time is a measure of perceptual distance between two images.
source: The reciprocal of response time is a measure of perceptual distance (or dissimilarity) between the two images (Arun, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arun, 2012.

claim: Representations reconstructed from behavioural data closely match population neural responses in high-level visual areas.
source: Such representations reconstructed from behavioural data closely match population neural responses in high-level visual areas (Op de Beeck et al., 2001; Sripati and Olson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Op de Beeck et al., 2001 and Sripati and Olson, 2010.

claim: In Experiment 2, 16 human participants performed a target present/absent search task inside an MRI scanner.
source: In Experiment 2, 16 human participants viewed an array of items on each trial, and indicated using a key press whether there was an oddball target present or not (Figure 3C). This task was performed inside an MRI scanner to simultaneously observe both brain activity and behaviour.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in Experiment 2.

claim: Participants in Experiment 2 were highly accurate (accuracy: 95 ± 3%).
source: Participants were highly accurate and consistent in their responses (accuracy, mean ± sd: 95 ± 3%; correlation between average response times of even- and odd-numbered participants: r=0.86, p<0.0001 across 32 target-present searches, r=0.63, p<0.001 across 32 target-absent searches).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Response times in Experiment 2 were consistent across participants for target-present searches (r=0.86, p<0.0001).
source: Participants were highly accurate and consistent in their responses (accuracy, mean ± sd: 95 ± 3%; correlation between average response times of even- and odd-numbered participants: r=0.86, p<0.0001 across 32 target-present searches, r=0.63, p<0.001 across 32 target-absent searches).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Response times in Experiment 2 were consistent across participants for target-absent searches (r=0.63, p<0.001).
source: Participants were highly accurate and consistent in their responses (accuracy, mean ± sd: 95 ± 3%; correlation between average response times of even- and odd-numbered participants: r=0.86, p<0.0001 across 32 target-present searches, r=0.63, p<0.001 across 32 target-absent searches).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Visual homogeneity of target-present arrays was significantly smaller than target-absent arrays.
source: As expected, the visual homogeneity of target-present arrays was significantly smaller than target-absent arrays (Figure 3E).
evidence: This reports experimental results with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Response times for target-present searches were positively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=0.68, p<0.0001).
source: The response times for target-present searches were positively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=0.68, p<0.0001; Figure 3F).
evidence: This reports experimental results with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: Response times for target-absent searches were negatively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=–0.71, p<0.0001).
source: By contrast, the response times for target-absent searches were negatively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=–0.71, p<0.0001; Figure 3G).
evidence: This reports experimental results with reference to Figure 3G.

claim: The range of visual homogeneity values for target-present and target-absent searches overlap.
source: We note that the range of visual homogeneity values for target-present and target-absent searches do overlap, suggesting that visual homogeneity contributes but does not fully determine task performance.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Visual homogeneity provides a useful initial first guess at the presence or absence of a target.
source: Rather, we suggest that visual homogeneity provides a useful and initial first guess at the presence or absence of a target, which can be refined further through detailed scrutiny.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Distance-to-center computations using deep neural network representations can predict target present/absent responses.
source: To confirm this, we replaced the object representations derived from Experiment 1 with object representations derived from deep neural networks pretrained for object categorization, and asked if distance-to-center computations could predict the target present/absent responses in Experiment 2. This was indeed the case (Appendix 1).
evidence: This reports additional analysis results referenced in Appendix 1.

claim: The nonlinear optimization process yields the same best-fitting center each time when repeated with many randomly initialized starting points.
source: To investigate this, we repeated the optimization procedure with many randomly initialized starting points, and obtained the same best-fitting center each time (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This reports a validation analysis of the optimization procedure.

claim: Leave-one-out cross validation yielded similar positive and negative correlations (r=0.63, p<0.0001 for target-present, r=–0.63, p<0.001 for target-absent).
source: To confirm that the above model fits are not due to overfitting, we performed a leave-one-out cross validation analysis. We left out all target-present and target-absent searches involving a particular image, and then predicted these searches by calculating visual homogeneity estimated from all other images. This too yielded similar positive and negative correlations (r=0.63, p<0.0001 for target-present, r=–0.63, p<0.001 for target-absent).
evidence: This reports cross-validation results.

claim: The average distance of an object from all other objects in visual search can predict its visual homogeneity.
source: We confirmed that this was indeed the case, suggesting that the average distance of an object from all other objects in visual search can predict its visual homogeneity (Appendix 2).
evidence: This reports additional analysis results referenced in Appendix 2.

claim: The best correlation between neural responses and behavior was obtained for almost equal weights of target and distractor in the lateral occipital region.
source: The best correlation was obtained for almost equal weights in the lateral occipital (LO) region, consistent with averaging and its role in the underlying perceptual representation (Appendix 2).
evidence: This reports analysis results referenced in Appendix 2.

claim: Visual homogeneity can explain oddball target present/absent judgements during visual search.
source: In sum, we conclude that visual homogeneity can explain oddball target present/absent judgements during visual search.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: 'Same' responses are correlated with target-absent judgements and 'different' responses are correlated with target-present judgements.
source: We therefore predicted that 'same' responses would be correlated with target-absent judgements and 'different' responses would be correlated with target-present judgements. Remarkably, this was indeed the case (Appendix 4), demonstrating that same/different responses can also be predicted using visual homogeneity.
evidence: This reports experimental results referenced in Appendix 4.

claim: Target-absent response times are unaffected by a variety of experimental context manipulations.
source: We performed a number of experiments to evaluate this possibility: we found that target-absent response times, which index visual homogeneity, are unaffected by a variety of experimental context manipulations (Appendix 5).
evidence: This reports experimental results referenced in Appendix 5.

claim: Visual homogeneity is an image-computable property that remains stable across tasks.
source: We therefore propose that visual homogeneity is an image-computable property that remains stable across tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Visual homogeneity can be empirically estimated as the reciprocal of the target-absent response times in a visual search task.
source: Moreover, it can be empirically estimated as the reciprocal of the target-absent response times in a visual search task.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion from the study.

claim: Visual homogeneity was encoded in a highly localized region just anterior of the lateral occipital region.
source: Visual homogeneity was encoded in a highly localized region just anterior of the lateral occipital (LO) region, with additional weak activations in the parietal and frontal regions.
evidence: This reports brain imaging results from Experiment 2.

claim: Visual homogeneity is encoded strongly in region VH and only weakly in other visual regions.
source: This revealed visual homogeneity to be encoded strongly in this region VH, and only weakly in other visual regions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The match between visual homogeneity and neural activations in the VH region remained significant even when the VH region was defined using one group of participants and the correlation was calculated using the mean activations of the other group.
source: Importantly, the match between mean activation and visual homogeneity remained significant even when the VH region was defined using one group of participants and the correlation was calculated using the mean activations of the other group (Appendix 6).
evidence: This reports cross-validation results referenced in Appendix 6.

claim: Mean activations in the VH region are uncorrelated with response times overall.
source: The resulting maps show that mean activations in the VH region are uncorrelated with response times overall (Appendix 6).
evidence: This reports brain imaging analysis results referenced in Appendix 6.

claim: Activations in EVC and LO are negatively correlated with response times.
source: By contrast, activations in EVC and LO are negatively correlated with response times, suggesting that faster responses are driven by higher activation of these areas.
evidence: This reports brain imaging analysis results.

claim: Mean activation of parietal and prefrontal regions were strongly correlated with response times, consistent with their role in attentional modulation.
source: Finally, mean activation of parietal and prefrontal regions were strongly correlated with response times, consistent with their role in attentional modulation (Appendix 6).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with interpretation based on known functions of these regions.

claim: Perceptual dissimilarities from visual search are best correlated in the lateral occipital region.
source: It can be seen that perceptual dissimilarities from visual search are best correlated in the lateral occipital region, consistent with previous studies (Figure 4E).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figure 4E and previous studies.

claim: Perceptual dissimilarities matched best with neural dissimilarities in LO compared to other visual regions.
source: Perceptual dissimilarities matched best with neural dissimilarities in LO compared to the other visual regions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This reports brain imaging analysis results with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Neural representations in LO match with perceptual space.
source: We conclude that neural representations in LO match with perceptual space. This is concordant with many previous studies (Haushofer et al., 2008; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Agrawal et al., 2020; Storrs et al., 2021; Ayzenberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the current data and multiple citations.

claim: Neural responses to target-present displays can be predicted as a linear sum of the constituent items with roughly equal weights for the target and distractor.
source: The resulting maps revealed that target-present arrays were accurately predicted as a linear sum of the constituent items, with roughly equal weights for the target and distractor (Appendix 6).
evidence: This reports brain imaging analysis results referenced in Appendix 6.

claim: In Experiment 3, participants performed searches involving all possible 2016 pairs of 64 objects.
source: Participants performed searches involving all possible 64C2=2016 pairs of objects.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in Experiment 3.

claim: Participants in Experiment 3 made highly accurate responses (accuracy: 98.5 ± 1.33%).
source: Participants made highly accurate and consistent responses on this task (accuracy, mean ± sd: 98.5 ± 1.33%; correlation between average response times from even- and odd-numbered subjects: r=0.88, p<0.0001 across 2016 searches).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Response times in Experiment 3 were consistent across participants (r=0.88, p<0.0001).
source: Participants made highly accurate and consistent responses on this task (accuracy, mean ± sd: 98.5 ± 1.33%; correlation between average response times from even- and odd-numbered subjects: r=0.88, p<0.0001 across 2016 searches).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Symmetric objects are generally more spread apart than asymmetric objects in perceptual space.
source: It can be seen that symmetric objects are generally more spread apart than asymmetric objects, suggesting that visual homogeneity could discriminate between symmetric and asymmetric objects.
evidence: This is an observation from the multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In Experiment 4, participants made accurate and consistent responses (accuracy: 97.7 ± 1.7%).
source: Participants made accurate and consistent responses in this task (accuracy, mean ± sd: 97.7 ± 1.7%; correlation between response times of odd- and even-numbered participants: r=0.47, p<0.0001).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Response times in Experiment 4 were consistent across participants (r=0.47, p<0.0001).
source: Participants made accurate and consistent responses in this task (accuracy, mean ± sd: 97.7 ± 1.7%; correlation between response times of odd- and even-numbered participants: r=0.47, p<0.0001).
evidence: This reports experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Visual homogeneity was significantly larger for symmetric compared to asymmetric objects (p<0.05).
source: As predicted, visual homogeneity was significantly larger for symmetric compared to asymmetric objects (visual homogeneity, mean ± sd: 0.60±0.24 s–1 for asymmetric objects; 0.76±0.29 s–1 for symmetric objects; p<0.05, rank-sum test; Figure 5E).
evidence: This reports experimental results with reference to Figure 5E.

claim: For asymmetric objects, symmetry detection response times were positively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=0.56, p<0.001).
source: For asymmetric objects, symmetry detection response times were positively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=0.56, p<0.001; Figure 5F).
evidence: This reports experimental results with reference to Figure 5F.

claim: For symmetric objects, response times were negatively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=–0.39, p<0.05).
source: By contrast, for symmetric objects, response times were negatively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=–0.39, p<0.05; Figure 5G).
evidence: This reports experimental results with reference to Figure 5G.

claim: The range of visual homogeneity values for asymmetric and symmetric objects overlap.
source: However, we note that the range of visual homogeneity values for asymmetric and symmetric objects do overlap, suggesting that visual homogeneity contributes but does not fully determine task performance.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Visual homogeneity provides a useful initial first guess at symmetry in an image.
source: We therefore propose that visual homogeneity provides a useful and initial first guess at symmetry in an image, which can be refined further through detailed scrutiny.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Leave-one-out cross validation for symmetry detection yielded similar correlations (r=0.44 for asymmetric, r=–0.39 for symmetric objects, p<0.05 in both cases).
source: To confirm that the above model fits are not due to overfitting, we performed a leave-one-out cross validation analysis, where we left out one object at a time, and then calculated its visual homogeneity. This too yielded similar correlations (r=0.44 for asymmetric, r=–0.39 for symmetric objects, p<0.05 in both cases).
evidence: This reports cross-validation results.

claim: Visual homogeneity can predict symmetry perception.
source: In sum, we conclude that visual homogeneity can predict symmetry perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The same computation (distance from a center) explains two disparate property-based visual tasks: symmetry perception and visual search.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that the same computation (distance from a center) explains two disparate property-based visual tasks: symmetry perception and visual search.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of Experiments 1-4.

claim: Visual homogeneity during symmetry detection is encoded in a localized region in the visual cortex as well as some parietal regions.
source: This revealed a localized region in the visual cortex as well as some parietal regions where this correlation attained a maximum (Figure 6A).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The VH region identified during symmetry detection overlaps with the VH region defined during visual search.
source: This VH region (average MNI coordinates (x, y, z): (−57,–56, –8) with 93 voxels in the left hemisphere; (58, -50, -8) with 73 voxels in the right hemisphere) overlaps with VH region defined during visual search in Experiment 3 (for a detailed comparison, see Appendix 8).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Appendix 8.

claim: Mean activations in the VH region during symmetry detection were poorly correlated with response times overall.
source: This revealed that mean activations in the VH region were poorly correlated with response times overall, whereas other parietal and prefrontal regions strongly correlated with response times, consistent with their role in attentional modulation and executive functions (Appendix 7).
evidence: This reports brain imaging analysis results referenced in Appendix 7.

claim: Parietal and prefrontal regions strongly correlated with response times during symmetry detection, consistent with their role in attentional modulation and executive functions.
source: This revealed that mean activations in the VH region were poorly correlated with response times overall, whereas other parietal and prefrontal regions strongly correlated with response times, consistent with their role in attentional modulation and executive functions (Appendix 7).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with interpretation based on known functions of these regions.

claim: The match between neural and perceptual dissimilarity during symmetry detection was maximum in the lateral occipital region.
source: The match between neural and perceptual dissimilarity was maximum in the lateral occipital region (Figure 6B).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The match with visual homogeneity during symmetry detection is best in the VH region compared to other regions.
source: This revealed that the match with visual homogeneity is best in the VH region compared to the other regions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Perceptual dissimilarities measured from visual search matched best with the LO region during symmetry detection.
source: This revealed that perceptual dissimilarities (measured from Experiment 3, during visual search) matched best with the LO region (Figure 6E), suggesting that object representations in LO are the basis for visual homogeneity computations in the VH region.
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figure 6E and includes an interpretation.

claim: Visual homogeneity is encoded by the VH region, using object representations present in the adjoining LO region.
source: In sum, our results suggest that visual homogeneity is encoded by the VH region, using object representations present in the adjoining LO region.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the brain imaging results.

claim: Target-absent response times predict symmetry detection with a positive correlation for asymmetric objects and a negative correlation for symmetric objects.
source: Specifically, since target-absent response time is inversely correlated with visual homogeneity, we can take its reciprocal as an estimate of visual homogeneity. This in turn predicts opposite correlations between symmetry detection times and reciprocal of target-absent response time: in other words, we should see a positive correlation for asymmetric objects, and a negative correlation for symmetric objects. We confirmed these predictions using additional experiments (Appendix 9).
evidence: This reports experimental results referenced in Appendix 9.

claim: A common decision variable, visual homogeneity, drives both target present/absent and symmetry judgements.
source: These results reconfirm that a common decision variable, visual homogeneity, drives both target present/absent and symmetry judgements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: By adjusting the center of the perceptual space, visual homogeneity can predict categorization responses for animals, dogs, and Labradors.
source: By adjusting the center of the perceptual space measured using visual search, we were able to predict categorization responses for all three categories (Appendix 10).
evidence: This reports analysis results referenced in Appendix 10.

claim: The default visual homogeneity, as indexed by the reciprocal of target-absent search time, can predict categorization responses.
source: We further reasoned that, if the optimum center for animal/dog/Labrador categorization is close to the default center in perceptual space that predicts target present/absent judgements, then even the default visual homogeneity, as indexed by the reciprocal of target-absent search time, should predict categorization responses. Interestingly, this was indeed the case (Appendix 10).
evidence: This reports analysis results referenced in Appendix 10.

claim: At least for the categories tested, visual homogeneity computations can serve as a decision variable for object categorization.
source: We conclude that, at least for the categories tested, visual homogeneity computations can serve as a decision variable for object categorization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis results.

claim: A single decision variable (visual homogeneity) can be used to solve three disparate visual tasks (visual search, same/different and symmetry detection).
source: Our main finding, that a single decision variable (visual homogeneity) can be used to solve three disparate visual tasks (visual search, same/different and symmetry detection) is novel to the best of our knowledge.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Visual homogeneity is the underlying decision variable at least for oddball visual search tasks.
source: Our results suggest that visual homogeneity is the underlying decision variable at least for oddball visual search tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Visual homogeneity could be an additional driving factor for making decisions during visual search.
source: Our findings suggest that visual homogeneity could also be an additional driving factor for making decisions during visual search.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The slope of target-absent search times as a function of set size are typically twice the slope of target present searches.
source: The slope of target-absent search times as a function of set size are typically twice the slope of target present searches (Wolfe, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolfe, 1998.

claim: Systematic variation in target-absent search is driven by visual homogeneity.
source: Our results resolve this puzzle by showing that this systematic variation is driven by visual homogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: We sometimes know a target is present without knowing its exact location because visual homogeneity arises in high-level visual areas with relatively coarse spatial information.
source: Finally, our findings also help explain why we sometimes know a target is present without knowing its exact location – this is because the underlying decision variable, visual homogeneity, arises in high-level visual areas with relatively coarse spatial information, and its computation does not entail knowledge of the oddball's location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the localization of visual homogeneity computations.

claim: Visual homogeneity computations do not completely explain all the variance observed in oddball search times.
source: However, we note that visual homogeneity computations described in this study do not completely explain all the variance observed in oddball search times in our study – rather they offer a quantitative model that could explain the initial phase of target selection.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the model.

claim: 'Same' responses are faster than 'different' responses in same-different tasks.
source: But in fact, 'same' responses are faster than 'different' responses.
evidence: This is a well-known observation in the literature on same-different tasks.

claim: Visual homogeneity can be used to implement a simple decision rule for making same/different responses.
source: Our findings resolve this puzzle by identifying a novel variable, visual homogeneity, which can be used to implement a simple decision rule for making same/different responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Visual homogeneity explains why some images elicit faster 'same' responses than others.
source: Our findings also explain why some images elicit faster 'same' responses than others: this is due to image-to-image differences in visual homogeneity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Most theoretical accounts of symmetry detection assume that symmetry is explicitly detected using symmetry detectors along particular axes.
source: Third, with regard to symmetry detection, most theoretical accounts assume that symmetry is explicitly detected using symmetry detectors along particular axes (Wagemans, 1997; Bertamini and Makin, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wagemans, 1997 and Bertamini and Makin, 2014.

claim: Visual homogeneity computations indicate an indirect mechanism for symmetry detection that does not invoke any special symmetry computations.
source: By contrast, our findings indicate an indirect mechanism for symmetry detection that does not invoke any special symmetry computations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Symmetric objects have high visual homogeneity since they have repeated parts.
source: This is because symmetric objects have high visual homogeneity since they have repeated parts, whereas asymmetric objects have low visual homogeneity since they have disparate parts (Pramod and Arun, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the definition of visual homogeneity and supported by citation to Pramod and Arun, 2018.

claim: Asymmetric objects have low visual homogeneity since they have disparate parts.
source: This is because symmetric objects have high visual homogeneity since they have repeated parts, whereas asymmetric objects have low visual homogeneity since they have disparate parts (Pramod and Arun, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the definition of visual homogeneity and supported by citation to Pramod and Arun, 2018.

claim: In a recent study, symmetry detection was explained by the average distance of objects relative to other objects.
source: In a recent study, symmetry detection was explained by the average distance of objects relative to other objects (Pramod and Arun, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pramod and Arun, 2018.

claim: Visual homogeneity is correlated with the average distance to other objects.
source: This finding is consistent with ours since visual homogeneity is correlated with the average distance to other objects (Appendix 1).
evidence: This reports analysis results referenced in Appendix 1.

claim: Visual homogeneity is an intrinsic image property.
source: Visual homogeneity is an intrinsic image property, whereas the average distance of an object to other objects depends on the set of other objects on which the average is being computed.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction made by the authors.

claim: Visual homogeneity is independent of experimental context.
source: Indeed, we have confirmed through additional experiments that visual homogeneity is independent of experimental context (Appendix 4).
evidence: This reports experimental results referenced in Appendix 4.

claim: Visual homogeneity can explain many other aspects of symmetry perception, such as the relative strength of symmetries.
source: We speculate that visual homogeneity can explain many other aspects of symmetry perception, such as the relative strength of symmetries.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Visual homogeneity can be easily extended to explain delayed match-to-sample tasks or n-back tasks.
source: First, we note that visual homogeneity can be easily extended to explain other property-based tasks such as delayed match-to-sample tasks or n-back tasks, by taking the response to the test stimulus as being averaged with the sample-related information in working memory.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Visual homogeneity can be extended to explain object categorization if the center in perceptual space can be temporarily shifted to the center of an object category.
source: Second, we note that visual homogeneity can also be extended to explain object categorization, if one assumes that the center in perceptual space for calculating visual homogeneity can be temporarily shifted to the center of an object category.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The idea that visual homogeneity can explain categorization is consistent with prevalent accounts of object categorization.
source: This idea is consistent with prevalent accounts of object categorization (Stewart and Morin, 2007; Ashby and Maddox, 2011; Mohan and Arun, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on object categorization.

claim: Categorization response times can be explained using perceptual distances to category and non-category items.
source: Indeed, categorization response times can be explained using perceptual distances to category and non-category items (Mohan and Arun, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mohan and Arun, 2012.

claim: Visual homogeneity is encoded in a specific region of the brain, denoted as region VH, in both visual search and symmetry detection tasks.
source: We have found that visual homogeneity is encoded in a specific region of the brain, which we denote as region VH, in both visual search and symmetry detection tasks (Figures 4D and 5D).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figures 4D and 5D.

claim: The finding of a dedicated region for visual homogeneity is consistent with observations of norm-based encoding in IT neurons.
source: This finding is consistent with observations of norm-based encoding in IT neurons (Leopold et al., 2006) and in face recognition (Valentine, 1991; Rhodes and Jeffery, 2006; Carlin and Kriegeskorte, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on norm-based encoding.

claim: The VH region is located just anterior to the lateral occipital (LO) region.
source: We have found that the VH region is located just anterior to the lateral occipital (LO) region, where neural dissimilarities match closely with perceptual dissimilarities (Figures 4E and 5E).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figures 4E and 5E.

claim: Visual homogeneity computations are based on object representations in LO.
source: Based on this proximity, we speculate that visual homogeneity computations are based on object representations in LO.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the proximity of VH and LO regions.

claim: Perturbing LO would distort the underlying representation, whereas perturbing VH would distort the underlying decision process.
source: A simple prediction would be that perturbing LO would distort the underlying representation, whereas perturbing VH would distort the underlying decision process.
evidence: This is a prediction for future causal experiments.

claim: The overall magnitude of the population neural response of monkey inferior temporal (IT) cortex neurons was found to correlate with memorability.
source: For instance, the overall magnitude of the population neural response of monkey inferior temporal (IT) cortex neurons was found to correlate with memorability (Jaegle et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaegle et al., 2019.

claim: Neural responses in IT cortex predict perceptual dissimilarities.
source: However, we note that neural responses in IT cortex also predict perceptual dissimilarities (Op de Beeck et al., 2001; Sripati and Olson, 2010; Zhivago and Arun, 2014; Agrawal et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Visual homogeneity computations and the underlying perceptual representation could be interleaved within a single neural population in monkeys.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that visual homogeneity computations and the underlying perceptual representation could be interleaved within a single neural population, unlike in humans where we found separate regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation comparing monkey and human data.

claim: The mean activations of the LO region were correlated with visual homogeneity for symmetry detection but not for target present/absent search.
source: Indeed, in our study, the mean activations of the LO region were also correlated with visual homogeneity for symmetry detection (Figure 6A), but not for target present/absent search (Figure 4A).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results with reference to Figures 4A and 6A.

claim: Visual homogeneity might be intermingled into the object representation in monkeys but separated into a dedicated region in humans.
source: We speculate that perhaps visual homogeneity might be intermingled into the object representation in monkeys but separated into a dedicated region in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation comparing monkey and human data.

claim: The localized activations in this study match closely with the location of the recently reported ventral stream attention module in both humans and monkeys.
source: The localized activations in our study match closely with the location of the recently reported ventral stream attention module in both humans and monkeys (Sani et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sani et al., 2021.

claim: Previous studies have observed larger brain activations for animate compared to inanimate objects in high-level visual areas.
source: First, previous studies have observed larger brain activations for animate compared to inanimate objects in high-level visual areas which have typically included the newly defined VH region reported here (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2015; Proklova et al., 2016; Thorat et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Visual homogeneity, as indexed by the reciprocal of target-absent search time, is smaller for animate objects compared to inanimate objects.
source: In our study, visual homogeneity, as indexed by the reciprocal of target-absent search time, is smaller for animate objects compared to inanimate objects (Appendix 9).
evidence: This reports analysis results referenced in Appendix 9.

claim: Brain activations were weaker for animate objects compared to inanimate objects in region VH.
source: Likewise, brain activations were weaker for animate objects compared to inanimate objects in region VH (average VH activations, mean ± sd across participants: 0.50±0.61 for animate target-absent displays, 0.64±0.59 for inanimate target-absent displays, p<0.05, sign-rank test across participants).
evidence: This reports brain imaging results.

claim: Visual homogeneity may be an additional organizing factor in human ventral temporal cortex.
source: Our results do however suggest that visual homogeneity may be an additional organizing factor in human ventral temporal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Previous studies have reported larger brain activations for symmetric objects compared to asymmetric objects in the vicinity of the VH region.
source: Second, previous studies have reported larger brain activations for symmetric objects compared to asymmetric objects in the vicinity of this region (Sasaki et al., 2005; Van Meel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sasaki et al., 2005 and Van Meel et al., 2019.

claim: Symmetric objects have larger visual homogeneity, leading to activation of the VH region.
source: This can be explained by our finding that symmetric objects have larger visual homogeneity (Figure 5E), leading to activation of the VH region (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the current results to previous findings.

claim: The results are consistent with the greater activity observed for objects with shared features in ventral temporal cortex during naming tasks.
source: Finally, our results are consistent with the greater activity observed for objects with shared features observed in ventral temporal cortex during naming tasks (Taylor et al., 2012; Tyler et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2012 and Tyler et al., 2013.

claim: Visual homogeneity may at least partially explain semantic concepts.
source: We speculate that visual homogeneity may at least partially explain semantic concepts such as those described in these studies.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Visual homogeneity refers to the distance of a visual image to a central point in the underlying perceptual representation.
source: We have defined a novel image property, visual homogeneity, which refers to the distance of a visual image to a central point in the underlying perceptual representation.
evidence: This is the definition of visual homogeneity provided by the authors.

claim: Visual homogeneity can be reliably estimated for each image as the inverse of the target-absent response time in a visual search task.
source: It can be reliably estimated for each image as the inverse of the target-absent response time in a visual search task (Figure 3) and seems to be an intrinsic image property that is unaffected by the immediate experimental context (Appendix 4).
evidence: This reports a methodological finding with reference to Figure 3 and Appendix 4.

claim: Visual homogeneity seems to be an intrinsic image property that is unaffected by the immediate experimental context.
source: It can be reliably estimated for each image as the inverse of the target-absent response time in a visual search task (Figure 3) and seems to be an intrinsic image property that is unaffected by the immediate experimental context (Appendix 4).
evidence: This reports experimental results referenced in Appendix 4.

claim: There are specific image properties that predict image memorability.
source: Recent studies have elucidated this observation by showing that there are specific image properties that predict image memorability (Bainbridge et al., 2017; Lukavský and Děchtěrenko, 2017; Rust and Mehrpour, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on image memorability.

claim: Image memorability could be driven by a number of both intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
source: However, image memorability, as elegantly summarized in a recent review (Rust and Mehrpour, 2020), could be driven by a number of both intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rust and Mehrpour, 2020.

claim: Saliency is empirically measured as the relative proportion of fixations towards an image.
source: Likewise, saliency is empirically measured as the relative proportion of fixations towards an image, and could be driven by top-down as well as by bottom-up factors (Eimer, 2014; Peelen and Kastner, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eimer, 2014 and Peelen and Kastner, 2014.

claim: Many property-based visual tasks can be solved using visual homogeneity as a decision variable, which is localized to a specific region anterior to the lateral occipital cortex.
source: Taken together, our results show that many property-based visual tasks can be solved using visual homogeneity as a decision variable, which is localized to a specific region anterior to the lateral occipital cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The study represents an important first step in demonstrating a quantitative, falsifiable model and a localized neural substrate for property-based visual tasks.
source: While this does not explain all possible variations of these tasks, our study represents an important first step in terms of demonstrating a quantitative, falsifiable model and a localized neural substrate.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the study.

claim: Visual homogeneity computations might contribute to a variety of other visual tasks.
source: We propose further that visual homogeneity computations might contribute to a variety of other visual tasks as well, and these would be interesting possibilities for future work.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All participants had a normal or corrected-to-normal vision and gave informed consent to an experimental protocol approved by the Institutional Human Ethics Committee of the Indian Institute of Science (IHEC # 6–15092017).
evidence: This describes the participant inclusion criteria.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Human Ethics Committee of the Indian Institute of Science.
source: All participants had a normal or corrected-to-normal vision and gave informed consent to an experimental protocol approved by the Institutional Human Ethics Committee of the Indian Institute of Science (IHEC # 6–15092017).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Participants provided written informed consent before each experiment and were monetarily compensated.
source: Participants provided written informed consent before each experiment and were monetarily compensated.
evidence: This describes the consent and compensation procedures.

claim: A total of 16 participants (8 males, 22±2.8 years) participated in Experiment 1.
source: A total of 16 participants (8 males, 22±2.8 years) participated in this experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 1.

claim: The stimulus set in Experiment 1 comprised 32 grayscale natural objects (16 animate, 16 inanimate) presented against a black background.
source: The stimulus set comprised a set of 32 grayscale natural objects (16 animate, 16 inanimate) presented against a black background.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, each trial began with a red fixation cross for 500ms, followed by a 4x4 search array for 5 s or until a response was made.
source: Each trial began with a red fixation cross (diameter 0.5°) for 500ms, followed by a 4x4 search array measuring 30° x 30° for 5 s or until a response was made.
evidence: This describes the trial structure in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, the search array always contained one oddball target and 15 identical distractors.
source: The search array always contained one oddball target and 15 identical distractors, with the target appearing equally often on the left or right.
evidence: This describes the display composition in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, incorrect trials were repeated later after a random number of other trials.
source: Incorrect trials were repeated later after a random number of other trials.
evidence: This describes the trial repetition procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: Each participant in Experiment 1 completed 992 correct trials.
source: Each participant completed 992 correct trials (32C2 object pairs x 2 repetitions with either image as target).
evidence: This describes the number of trials in Experiment 1.

claim: The experiment in Experiment 1 was created using PsychoPy and ported to the online platform Pavlovia for collecting data.
source: The experiment was created using PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) and ported to the online platform Pavlovia for collecting data.
evidence: This describes the software used for Experiment 1.

claim: Stimulus size in Experiment 1 was equated across participants using the ScreenScale function.
source: Since stimulus size could vary with the monitor used by the online participants, we equated the stimulus size across participants using the ScreenScale function (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/8FHQK).
evidence: This describes the stimulus size calibration procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: Response times faster than 0.3 s or slower than 3 s were removed from the data in Experiment 1.
source: Response times faster than 0.3 s or slower than 3 s were removed from the data. This step removed only 1.25% of the data and improved the overall response time consistency, but did not qualitatively alter the results.
evidence: This describes the data cleaning procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: The inverse of response time represents the dissimilarity between the target and distractor.
source: This inverse of response time (i.e. 1/RT) represents the dissimilarity between the target and distractor (Arun, 2012), indexes the underlying salience signal in visual search (Sunder and Arun, 2016) and combines linearly across a variety of factors (Pramod and Arun, 2014; Pramod and Arun, 2016; Jacob and Arun, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The inverse of response time indexes the underlying salience signal in visual search.
source: This inverse of response time (i.e. 1/RT) represents the dissimilarity between the target and distractor (Arun, 2012), indexes the underlying salience signal in visual search (Sunder and Arun, 2016) and combines linearly across a variety of factors (Pramod and Arun, 2014; Pramod and Arun, 2016; Jacob and Arun, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sunder and Arun, 2016.

claim: The inverse of response time combines linearly across a variety of factors.
source: This inverse of response time (i.e. 1/RT) represents the dissimilarity between the target and distractor (Arun, 2012), indexes the underlying salience signal in visual search (Sunder and Arun, 2016) and combines linearly across a variety of factors (Pramod and Arun, 2014; Pramod and Arun, 2016; Jacob and Arun, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pramod and Arun, 2014; Pramod and Arun, 2016; Jacob and Arun, 2020.

claim: A total of 16 subjects (11 males; age 25±2.9 years) participated in Experiment 2.
source: A total of 16 subjects (11 males; age, mean ± sd: 25±2.9 years) participated in this experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 2.

claim: Participants with history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, or with metal implants or claustrophobia were excluded from Experiment 2.
source: Participants with history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, or with metal implants or claustrophobia were excluded through screening questionnaires.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for Experiment 2.

claim: Inside the scanner in Experiment 2, participants performed a single run of a one-back task for functional localizers and eight runs of the present-absent search task.
source: Inside the scanner, participants performed a single run of a one-back task for functional localizers (block design, object vs scrambled objects), eight runs of the present-absent search task (event-related design), and an anatomical scan.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in Experiment 2.

claim: The experiment in Experiment 2 was deployed using custom MATLAB scripts written using Psychophysics Toolbox.
source: The experiment was deployed using custom MATLAB scripts written using Psychophysics Toolbox (Brainard, 1997).
evidence: This describes the software used for Experiment 2.

claim: In the functional localizer runs of Experiment 2, participants viewed a series of images and pressed a response button whenever an item was repeated.
source: Participants had to view a series of images against a black background and press a response button whenever an item was repeated.
evidence: This describes the task in the functional localizer runs of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, each search array had eight items arranged in a 3x3 grid with no central element.
source: Each search array had eight items, measuring 1.5° along the longer dimension, arranged in a 3x3 grid, with no central element to avoid fixation biases (as shown in Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes the display composition in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, each trial lasted 4 s (1 s ON time and 3 s OFF time).
source: Each trial lasted 4 s (1 s ON time and 3 s OFF time), and participants had to respond within 4 s.
evidence: This describes the trial timing in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, each run had 64 unique searches (32 present, 32 absent) presented in random order.
source: Each run had 64 unique searches (32 present, 32 absent) presented in random order, using the natural objects from Experiment 1.
evidence: This describes the trial composition in Experiment 2.

claim: Functional MRI data in Experiment 2 were acquired using a 32-channel head coil on a 3T Skyra at the HealthCare Global Hospital, Bengaluru.
source: Functional MRI (fMRI) data were acquired using a 32-channel head coil on a 3T Skyra (Siemens, Mumbai, India) at the HealthCare Global Hospital, Bengaluru.
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition setup for Experiment 2.

claim: The raw fMRI data in Experiment 2 were preprocessed using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) software Version 12.
source: The raw fMRI data were preprocessed using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) software (Version12; Welcome Center for Human Neuroimaging; https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software /spm12/), running on MATLAB 2019b.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing software for Experiment 2.

claim: The data in Experiment 2 were further processed using GLMdenoise.
source: The data were further processed using GLMdenoise (Kay et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes additional preprocessing steps for Experiment 2.

claim: GLMdenoise improves the signal-to-noise ratio in the data by regressing out the noise estimated from task-unrelated voxels.
source: GLMdenoise improves the signal-to-noise ratio in the data by regressing out the noise estimated from task-unrelated voxels.
evidence: This describes the function of GLMdenoise.

claim: Response times faster than 0.3 s or slower than 3 s were removed from the data in Experiment 2.
source: Response times faster than 0.3 s or slower than 3 s were removed from the data. This step removed only 0.75% of the data and improved the overall response time consistency, but did not qualitatively alter the results.
evidence: This describes the data cleaning procedure in Experiment 2.

claim: The model for visual homogeneity has only five free parameters, which are the coordinates of the center point in multidimensional space.
source: Note that this model has only five free parameters, which are the coordinates of this unknown point or center in multidimensional space, and this model can simultaneously predict both target-present and target-absent judgments.
evidence: This describes the model parameters.

claim: The optimum center for visual homogeneity remained stable across many random starting points.
source: This optimum center remained stable across many random starting points, and our results were qualitatively similar upon varying the number of embedding dimensions.
evidence: This reports a validation analysis of the optimization procedure.

claim: The absolute sum of the correlations between visual homogeneity and present/absent reaction times increased monotonically from 1 to 5 neurons, remained at a steady level from 5 to 9 neurons and decreased beyond 9 neurons.
source: We found that the absolute sum of the correlations between visual homogeneity and present/absent reaction times increased monotonically from 1 to 5 neurons, remained at a steady level from 5 to 9 neurons and decreased beyond 9 neurons.
evidence: This reports analysis results for selecting the number of dimensions.

claim: 5 neurons or dimensions were selected for reporting visual homogeneity computations.
source: We therefore selected 5 neurons or dimensions for reporting visual homogeneity computations.
evidence: This describes the methodological choice for the number of dimensions.

claim: A total of 15 participants (11 males, 22.8±4.3 years) participated in Experiment 3.
source: A total of 15 participants (11 males, 22.8±4.3 years) participated in this experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 3.

claim: Participants in Experiment 3 completed 4032 correct trials.
source: Participants completed 4032 correct trials (64C2 shape pairs x 2 repetitions) as two sessions in 2 days.
evidence: This describes the number of trials in Experiment 3.

claim: A total of 64 baton shapes (32 symmetric and 32 asymmetric) were used in Experiment 3.
source: We used a total of 64 baton shapes (32 symmetric and 32 asymmetric), and all shapes were presented against a black background.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in Experiment 3.

claim: 32 unique parts were created with the vertical line as part of the contour in Experiment 3.
source: We created 32 unique parts with the vertical line as part of the contour.
evidence: This describes the stimulus creation procedure in Experiment 3.

claim: 32 symmetric objects were created by joining the part and its mirror-filled version in Experiment 3.
source: We created 32 symmetric by joining the part and its mirror-filled version, and 32 asymmetric objects were created by randomly pairing the left part and mirror flipped version of another left part.
evidence: This describes the stimulus creation procedure in Experiment 3.

claim: 32 asymmetric objects were created by randomly pairing the left part and mirror flipped version of another left part in Experiment 3.
source: We created 32 symmetric by joining the part and its mirror-filled version, and 32 asymmetric objects were created by randomly pairing the left part and mirror flipped version of another left part.
evidence: This describes the stimulus creation procedure in Experiment 3.

claim: A total of 15 subjects participated in Experiment 4.
source: A total of 15 subjects participated in this study.
evidence: This describes the participant number for Experiment 4.

claim: Data from one participant in Experiment 4 were excluded due to poor accuracy and long response times.
source: We excluded the data from one participant due to poor accuracy and long response times.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion in Experiment 4.

claim: Inside the scanner in Experiment 4, participants performed two runs of one-back identity task and eight runs of symmetry judgment task.
source: Inside the scanner, participants performed two runs of one-back identity task (functional localizer), eight runs of symmetry judgment task (event-related design), and one anatomical scan.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, objects measured 4° and were presented against a black background.
source: Objects measured 4° and were presented against a black background.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, each trial lasted 4 s, with the object displayed for 200ms followed by a blank period of 3800ms.
source: Each trial lasted 4 s, with the object displayed for 200ms followed by a blank period of 3800ms.
evidence: This describes the trial timing in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, each run had 64 unique conditions (32 symmetric and 32 asymmetric).
source: Each run had 64 unique conditions (32 symmetric and 32 asymmetric).
evidence: This describes the trial composition in Experiment 4.

claim: Very fast (<100ms) reaction times were removed from the data in Experiment 4.
source: Very fast (<100ms) reaction times were removed.
evidence: This describes the data cleaning procedure in Experiment 4.

claim: All reaction times to an object were discarded if participant's accuracy was less than 80% in Experiment 4.
source: We also discarded all reaction times to an object if participant's accuracy was less than 80%. This process removed 3.6% of RT data.
evidence: This describes the data cleaning procedure in Experiment 4.

claim: The data cleaning process in Experiment 4 removed 3.6% of RT data.
source: We also discarded all reaction times to an object if participant's accuracy was less than 80%. This process removed 3.6% of RT data.
evidence: This reports the amount of data removed in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the oddball detection response times were embedded into multidimensional space with three dimensions.
source: We proceeded as before by embedding the oddball detection response times into multidimensional space with three dimensions.
evidence: This describes the analysis procedure for Experiment 4.
